* ### Parents Need to Know

  Parents need to know that Lego Builder's Journey is a downloadable puzzle game for Apple Arcade. The game is founded on Lego building blocks. It's viewed from an raised perspective and has no violence. The goal of the game is to guide a builder by finding, manipulating, and placing bricks to build things and create paths for the hero to traverse. Players are rewarded for thinking both logically and creatively -- many puzzles can be solved multiple ways. Kids familiar with Lego will intuitively understand how to play, and may come away from the game with the impulse to go play with (or buy, though the game contains no ads or calls to purchase) physical Lego kits.
* ### Products & Purchases

  a little

  This game features familiar Lego building blocks, but contains no ads or incentives to shop for real-world products.
* ### Positive Messages

  some

  Subtle themes of respect, individuality, and breaking free of molds run through the somewhat vague story. Play rewards logical thinking and a willingness to experiment.
* ### Positive Role Models

  some

  The builder is a problem solver, using wits and creativity (supplied by the player) to overcome obstacles in constructive, non-violent ways. He's also an eager learner, but capable of working independently.
* ### Ease of Play

  some

  Tutorial levels contain no written or audible instructions. Players must learn through trial, error, and observation. But the mechanics are simple enough that most kids shouldn't experience too much trouble.

## What's It About?

LEGO BUILDER'S JOURNEY is a puzzle adventure that sees players manipulating virtual Lego blocks to create simple structures and paths for the game's hero to traverse. Each level is essentially a floating Lego island with one or more incomplete areas that players must fix in order to progress. Kids might need to place golden bricks to create a trail for the builder to hop across, or assemble some twigs and a light-up stud to create a fire for him to sleep near. No instructions are provided, which means learning is a matter of trial and error, but most puzzles can be solved in a variety of ways and the mechanics are surprisingly simple. Just touch the screen near a piece to pick it up, slide your finger to move it into position, and hold still to click it into place. Part of the challenge is to find and identify pieces you can interact with and figure out where they might be usefully placed. As puzzles are solved, the builder's story progresses, and we see him move from eager student to independent problem solver.

## Is It Any Good?

**Our review:**

**Parents say** : Not yet rated

**Kids say :** Not yet rated

It's hard not to appreciate this game's relaxing vibe. Lego Builder's Journey is a more or less wordless experience, leading us through its indistinct yet uplifting story via images composed of colorful backgrounds, photorealistic Lego bricks, and the cute animations of its primary hero, who isn't a traditional Lego minifigure but rather an assembly of little Lego pieces roughly shaped to resemble an explorer. By the time you become accustomed to the adorableness of everything, you'll likely be hooked on the simple but compelling puzzles, which are typically pretty straightforward but nonetheless enjoyable. Clicking these digital pieces into place is just as satisfying as doing the same to their counterparts in the real world, and may even give imaginative kids some new ideas for models to build with their own bin of plastic bricks. That most puzzles have multiple potential solutions will only serve to stoke players' imaginations.

The only time the experience stutters is when timing becomes a factor. Making a piece settle into the proper place takes a little patience as you maneuver it just so and then wait for a second or two for it to click. Most of the time, this isn't an issue, but if you, say, need to create a path of bricks on the ground that begins to fall as soon as a brick is laid on it, then repeatedly do it again, it can start to become a little tense and frustrating. Happily, not all puzzles have timing elements, and in those that do, failure simply means picking up the pieces and trying again. This one snag aside, Lego Builder's Journey is a short but beautiful little puzzler that captures the spirit of the iconic toy on which it's founded almost perfectly.

## Talk to Your Kids About ...

* Families can talk about [screen time](/articles/screen-time). Lego Builder's Journey is a short game, but would you rather experience all the puzzles at once, or work through them just a few at a time so it lasts longer?
* What advantages come with making things physically compared to on a screen? What benefits do you gain from building stuff in a virtual world?

# LEGO® Fortnite® Parents’ Guide

![]()

Since its debut in December 2023, LEGO® Fortnite® has been growing and changing. And things just got a lot bigger and more exciting.

Today, LEGO Fortnite is more than a crafting-survival game. It’s an umbrella term and its own category within Epic Games’ Fortnite for a series of family-friendly LEGO games and experiences available for free. And as things continue to expand, one thing remains the same: our mission to empower play and creativity in a safe and secure environment for kids.

In this guide, written for parents of LEGO Fortnite players, we’ll explain the expanding LEGO Fortnite suite of experiences, how we can work together to help keep players safe, how to play with friends in LEGO Fortnite experiences, and show you how LEGO Fortnite has moved beyond the digital into the physical world.

## Understanding LEGO Fortnite

LEGO Fortnite is really a constellation of separate but cool LEGO experiences for everyone, including kids and families, all of which are available from within developer Epic Games’ Fortnite. Where you can download Fortnite – a game available on a wide variety of platforms, from video game consoles to PCs to mobile devices – you can also play the various LEGO Fortnite games.

There are three broad categories of LEGO Fortnite experiences to enjoy on [Android](https://www.fortnite.com/mobile/android), [iOS](https://www.epicgames.com/help/c-Category_Fortnite/c-Fortnite_TechnicalSupport/how-do-i-install-fortnite-on-ios-or-ipados-a000090666) (in the EU only), [Nintendo Switch™](https://www.epicgames.com/help/c-Category_Fortnite/c-Fortnite_Gameplay/how-to-download-fortnite-on-nintendo-switch-a000086670), [PlayStation](https://www.epicgames.com/help/c-Category_Fortnite/c-Fortnite_Gameplay/how-to-download-fortnite-on-playstation-a000086672), [PC](https://www.epicgames.com/help/c-Category_Fortnite/c-Fortnite_Gameplay/how-to-download-fortnite-on-pc-a000086666) and [Xbox](https://www.epicgames.com/help/c-Category_Fortnite/c-Fortnite_Gameplay/how-to-download-fortnite-on-xbox-a000086669).

**LEGO Fortnite Odyssey®, previously known as LEGO Fortnite**, is the game that started it all. It’s set in vast open worlds, unique to each player. Survival and Expert modes challenge players to craft and fight and build and eat to survive and thrive in challenging environments. Sandbox and Cozy modes remove most of the survival challenges and allow players to focus on exploring, experimenting and building with what amounts to a bottomless box of LEGO bricks and elements.

**LEGO Fortnite Islands** are an archipelago of smaller, focused experiences constructed with many of the same elements as LEGO Fortnite Odyssey. For example, LEGO Chasers vs Hunters is a competitive, team-based shooter where players battle with playful weapons in an arena inspired by Candy Realm from Season 1 of the LEGO DREAMzzz™ TV show. On the opposite end of the spectrum, LEGO Cat Island Adventure is a carefree, cozy experience where players visit an island full of cats to feed, pet and befriend. LEGO Cat Island Adventure, LEGO Chasers vs Hunters and other LEGO Fortnite Islands were created by the LEGO Group. Many more are available to play, thanks to Fortnite creators – players who also build their own experiences within the game. To learn more, be sure to read [everything you need to know about LEGO Islands in Fortnite](https://www.lego.com/themes/fortnite/lego-islands).

**LEGO Fortnite Brick Life** is the newest addition to the family, where players enter a city called Brick Bay, which is made of LEGO bricks. Players hang out and socialize, take on jobs, decorate their houses and unlock vehicles with the money they earn. Explore diverse locations like the beach, a bustling downtown and an eerie hillside Academy.

LEGO Fortnite has something for every player and every interest.

## You can play LEGO Fortnite together with friends

Each LEGO Fortnite experience is playable alone, but the best way to play the game is with friends. That’s easy to do with the built-in crossplay feature, which lets players cooperate and compete across the boundaries of consoles, PCs and mobile devices. Everyone can play together, no matter what hardware they’re using.

The LEGO Group and Epic Games have extensive parental controls that empower you to customize your kids’ experiences. You can learn more about them and how LEGO Fortnite creates a safe and secure environment in [our guide to playing with friends in LEGO Fortnite](https://www.lego.com/themes/fortnite/playing-with-friends-in-lego-fortnite).

## LEGO Fortnite safety

There are many ways that LEGO Fortnite games allow for age-appropriate experiences

LEGO Fortnite Odyssey, LEGO Fortnite Brick Life and each LEGO Fortnite Island includes an age rating. For players in the United States, they include an [ESRB rating](https://www.esrb.org/ratings-guide/). For players in most of Europe, they include a [PEGI rating](https://pegi.info/page/pegi-age-ratings). You can find the age rating of each LEGO experience in the Fortnite launcher. You can learn more about the parental control options and ratings in our [LEGO Fortnite Odyssey parents’ guide](https://www.lego.com/article/lego-odyssey-parents-guide), our [LEGO Fortnite Brick Life parents’ guide](https://www.lego.com/article/lego-brick-life-parents-guide) and our [guide to LEGO Fortnite Islands](https://www.lego.com/themes/fortnite/lego-islands).

Fortnite offers extensive parental controls that empower adults to manage their kids’ LEGO Fortnite experiences. That includes settings for voice and text chat permissions, settings to prevent real-money purchases, settings for controlling friend requests and settings that control which LEGO Fortnite experiences your child can play based on age ratings.

You should also know that each platform or console – [Android (Google Play)](https://support.google.com/googleplay/answer/1075738), [Epic Games](https://www.epicgames.com/id/login?redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.epicgames.com%2Faccount%2Fpersonal), [PlayStation](https://www.playstation.com/support/account/ps5-parental-controls-spending-limits/), [Xbox](https://support.xbox.com/help/family-online-safety/browse), [Nintendo Switch](https://www.nintendo.com/switch/parental-controls/) and [Windows](https://support.microsoft.com/account-billing/filter-apps-and-games-with-microsoft-edge-da38c83a-0717-31ea-b6f2-6cdd95639189) – also offers its own parental controls.

You can find detailed instructions for creating accounts and setting up parental controls in our [LEGO Fortnite Odyssey parents’ guide](https://www.lego.com/article/lego-odyssey-parents-guide) and our [LEGO Fortnite Brick Life parents’ guide](https://www.lego.com/article/lego-brick-life-parents-guide).

## LEGO Fortnite sets

![]()

LEGO Fortnite also exists in the real world, thanks to several physical LEGO Fortnite sets that include characters and items from the game.

[LEGO Fortnite Battle Bus](https://www.lego.com/product/battle-bus-77073) is a 954-piece set designed for builders 10+. It has rolling wheels, a removable roof and the game’s iconic hot-air balloon. The set also includes nine minifigures that longtime players will recognize. Those include Adventure Peely, Battalion Brawler, Brite Bomber, Cube Assassin, Cuddle Team Leader, Drift, Meowscles, Raven and Trespasser Elite.

[LEGO Fortnite Durrr Burger](https://www.lego.com/product/durrr-burger-77070) is a 193-piece set designed for builders 9+. It includes the eyes, olive, tongue and toothpick you’d expect to find on the iconic Fortnite fast-food mascot.

[LEGO Fortnite Peely](https://www.lego.com/product/peely-bone-77072) is a set designed for adult LEGO fans. With 1,414 pieces, it features movable arms and details that include the Banana Bag Back Bling, Paint Launcher and Peely Pick Pickaxe.

[LEGO Fortnite Supply Llama](https://www.lego.com/product/supply-llama-77071) is a 691-piece set and designed for builders 12+. Inside the box, you’ll find LEGO Fortnite items like a Backpack, Dynamite, Good Luck Charm, Grappler, Rough Ruby, Slap Juice and Slurp Juice.

The first batch of physical LEGO Fortnite sets were released in October 2024. Each of them is available now, exclusively in the LEGO Shop. Head over to the [LEGO Fortnite Sets page](https://www.lego.com/themes/fortnite) to check them all out and see the details and images of the gaming toys that we described above.

## LEGO®: Builder’s Journey [Review]

4–5 minutes

**Categories:** [Lego](https://ramblingbrick.com/category/lego/), [Review](https://ramblingbrick.com/category/review/), [Video Game](https://ramblingbrick.com/category/review/video-game/)

**Tags:** [Builder's Journey](https://ramblingbrick.com/tag/builders-journey/), [Game review](https://ramblingbrick.com/tag/game-review/), [LEGO Builder's Journey](https://ramblingbrick.com/tag/lego-builders-journey/), [Light Brick Studios](https://ramblingbrick.com/tag/light-brick-studios/), [readwritehand](https://ramblingbrick.com/tag/readwritehand/), [Video game](https://ramblingbrick.com/tag/video-game/)

*We have a guest contributor today. While I play a few games on my phone, my son Harry has experienced a far greater range of diverse games iacross a variety of platforms. I thought it would be helpful to get his opinion on LEGO® Builder’s Journey – the debut game from Light Brick Studios. His opinion might be a little different to mine… and that’s OK. Read on for his take on the game…*

**Lego: Builder’s Journey**

**Developer:** Light Brick Studio

**Platforms:** PC (Steam and Epic Games), Switch, iOS/Apple Arcade

**Genre:** Puzzle

**Replayability:** Low – Medium (depending on future updates)

 

Screenshots PC version. GTX Graphics

  

*LEGO: Builder’s Journey*by Light Brick Studio is a meditative puzzle game about the relationship between parent and child, the importance of play, and how cool LEGO is. From an aesthetic standpoint, it’s brilliant; the music and level design give a sense of serene contemplation even during the more frustrating levels, the unspoken story between the son and father was kind of heartwarming and even without the RTX graphics the levels look beautiful, from the broader strokes like the level design – the flowing rivers, treacherous mountains, and hidden caves – to the finer details, like the little scratches on the pieces and the way light reflects off them or shines through. Creative Director of Light Brick Studio, Karsten Lund, spoke in a [roundtable discussion](https://ramblingbrick.com/2021/07/13/going-on-a-builders-journey-with-light-brick-studios-fan-media-round-table/) on the game about how in the process of writing the narrative they “decided that we were not writing a story, we’re writing a poem” and this certainly comes across in the end product. Spiritually it feels almost akin to *Unravel* (2016), another puzzle game that relied on atmosphere to convey the story and emotion without dialogue.

From a mechanical standpoint, however, I have some slight gripes. The lack of dialogue works fine for the story, but there were several points throughout the game that I feel could have done with some additional tutorial, such as the bit where you have to construct a path by placing tiles which then multiply into other tiles and so on, which fails to make it clear that even though you’ve built a path the start of it is too high for you to cross despite the fact that other levels have allowed you to scale that height before, or even on occasion where it is you’re meant to be building a path to. The distinct beginning and end of each section is a bit of a disappointment too, as it often seems we’ve just gotten to grips with a mechanic and then it’s never brought up again, and given the shorter length (about three hours for me to complete it on PC) it would’ve been nice to see some of the mechanics integrated with each other a bit more*.*For a game about Lego, it ironically could’ve stood to build on itself a bit more.

That being said, the game’s still functional and enjoyable, and while the $30 price tag on PC and Switch initially seems a bit steep, it’s a marked improvement on the mobile version in terms of both graphics and controls. Light Brick have stated their intention to continue development and support for *Builder’s Journey*, which will hopefully include more levels or support for user-created ones, but if I take future content into account in a review then it’s difficult to have any confidence in it. A game could turn my computer to a pile of molten slag but I’d have to add the proviso that they might patch in a fire extinguisher. As-is, the game is good but the length and separation of mechanics from level to level makes it difficult to unconditionally recommend the PC and console versions at the current price at time of writing. If you’ve got Apple Arcade and don’t mind the slightly fiddly controls, however, that becomes significantly easier to recommend.

But if the time that you spend contains a high quality experience, surely that means for something. It probably depends on your personal dedication to the brick. If thinking about LEGO bricks dominates your day, then the price may be less material to you, especially if playing through Apple Arcade – either on mobile or iOS, rather than a direct purchase through Steam, Epic or Nintendo eStore. However, the difference between the images on the PC, with good video processing, or even better RTX graphics cannot be denied. If you are looking for ‘merely’ a casual gaming experience, this might not be for you.*

If you want to read more about the development process for the game, you can check out our write up of a [Fan Media Roundtable with the Development team,](https://ramblingbrick.com/2021/07/13/going-on-a-builders-journey-with-light-brick-studios-fan-media-round-table/) published earlier today.

# Understanding ESRB and PEGI Rating Systems: A Quick Guide

Learn what E, T, and M ratings actually mean for your child's games. We decode the symbols and content descriptors so you can play it safe.

Updated 5/13/26

# ESRB & PEGI Ratings Explained: The Ultimate Parent's Guide

**TL;DR**: Those letter ratings on game boxes? They're actually useful once you understand them. ESRB (North America) and PEGI (Europe) tell you age appropriateness AND specific content warnings. E10+ means mild cartoon violence, M means what you think it means, and T is the tricky middle ground where most parent arguments happen. Learn the system, check the content descriptors on the back, and you'll know exactly what you're buying before the first "Mom, can I get this?" at Target.

You're standing in the game aisle, your kid is holding up [Fortnite](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/fortnite-game) or the latest [Call of Duty](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/call-of-duty-game), and you're squinting at a little box on the corner that says "T" or "M" or "PEGI 16." What does any of this actually mean? And more importantly, should you trust it?

The short answer: yes, mostly. These ratings aren't perfect, but they're a solid starting point that can save you from accidentally buying your 8-year-old a game with graphic violence or your teen a game that's genuinely too mature even for them.

What Are ESRB and PEGI Ratings?

**ESRB** (Entertainment Software Rating Board) is the rating system used in North America. It's been around since 1994, created after Congress got concerned about violent games like Mortal Kombat. Think of it like the MPAA ratings for movies (G, PG, PG-13, R), but for games.

**PEGI** (Pan European Game Information) is the European equivalent, used across most of Europe and some other countries. It works similarly but has slightly different age categories and symbols.

Both systems do two things:

1. Give you an **age rating** (the big letter or number on the front)
2. List **content descriptors** (the specific stuff inside that earned that rating)

The age rating is what catches your eye. The content descriptors are what actually matter.

ESRB Ratings Breakdown

### E (Everyone)

Think [Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game) in peaceful mode or [Mario Kart](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/mario-kart-game). Suitable for all ages. Might have minimal cartoon violence (like bouncing on a Goomba's head), but nothing that would make you flinch.

### E10+ (Everyone 10+)

This is where you start seeing more action. Games like [Super Smash Bros](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/super-smash-bros-game) or [Splatoon](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/splatoon-game) land here. Mild cartoon violence, some comic mischief, minimal suggestive themes. Most kids 8-10 can handle this content, but the rating gives you a heads-up that it's not quite as innocent as pure E-rated games.

### T (Teen)

**This is where it gets interesting.** T-rated games are for ages 13+, but in practice, this is the most debated category among parents. [Fortnite](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/fortnite-game) is T-rated. So is [Apex Legends](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/apex-legends-game). So is [The Sims 4](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/the-sims-4-game).

T-rated games can include:

* Violence (but not super graphic)
* Suggestive themes
* Crude humor
* Minimal blood
* Simulated gambling
* Infrequent strong language

The range here is HUGE. Some T-rated games are fine for mature 11-year-olds. Others are genuinely pushing the boundary of what should be M-rated. **Always check the content descriptors on the back of the box.**

### M (Mature 17+)

Intense violence, blood and gore, sexual content, strong language. Games like [Grand Theft Auto](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/grand-theft-auto-game), [Red Dead Redemption](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/red-dead-redemption-game), most [Call of Duty](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/call-of-duty-game) games.

If your 12-year-old is asking for an M-rated game, [you can dig into whether it's appropriate for your family![](/favicons/favicon-32x32.png)](https://chat.screenwiseapp.com/?prompt=should%20I%20let%20my%2012%20year%20old%20play%20M%20rated%20games), but know that these ratings exist for a reason. The content is genuinely mature.

### AO (Adults Only 18+)

Extremely rare. Prolonged graphic violence, explicit sexual content, or real gambling. Most major retailers won't even stock AO games. If you see this rating, it's a hard no for kids.

PEGI Ratings Breakdown

PEGI uses numbers instead of letters, which is honestly more straightforward:

* **PEGI 3**: Suitable for all ages (like ESRB E)
* **PEGI 7**: May contain mild violence or scary scenes (like ESRB E10+, but younger)
* **PEGI 12**: Violence in a fantasy setting, mild bad language (similar to ESRB T, but more conservative)
* **PEGI 16**: Realistic violence, strong language, sexual innuendo (like ESRB T/M boundary)
* **PEGI 18**: Graphic violence, strong language, sexual content, drugs (like ESRB M)

PEGI also uses **content icons** on the front of the box showing what earned the rating: violence, bad language, fear, drugs, sex, discrimination, gambling, in-game purchases.

The Content Descriptors Matter More Than the Age Rating

Here's what most parents miss: **the age rating is just a suggestion. The content descriptors tell you what's actually in the game.**

A T-rated game might say:

* "Fantasy Violence"
* "Mild Blood"
* "Comic Mischief"

That's very different from a T-rated game that says:

* "Violence"
* "Blood"
* "Suggestive Themes"
* "Strong Language"

Both are rated T, but one is clearly more intense. Always flip the box over (or look up the rating online) and read what specific content is included.

Common content descriptors to understand:

* **Fantasy Violence** = not realistic (cartoon fighting, magic battles)
* **Violence** = more realistic depictions
* **Blood** = you'll see red
* **Intense Violence** = graphic, sustained, realistic
* **Suggestive Themes** = sexual innuendo, flirting, revealing outfits
* **Sexual Content** = actual sexual situations
* **Strong Language** = the F-word and similar
* **Crude Humor** = bathroom jokes, gross-out comedy
* **Use of Alcohol/Tobacco/Drugs** = characters using substances

What About Online Interactions?

You'll see "Online Interactions Not Rated by the ESRB" on almost every multiplayer game. This is critical to understand: **the rating system only covers the game content itself, not what other players might say or do.**

[Roblox](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/roblox-game) might be rated E10+, but if your kid is playing with randoms online, they could encounter inappropriate language, bullying, or worse. [Fortnite](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/fortnite-game) is T-rated for violence, but the voice chat can be way more mature than the game itself.

This is why [parental controls and communication matter![](/favicons/favicon-32x32.png)](https://chat.screenwiseapp.com/?prompt=how%20to%20set%20up%20parental%20controls%20for%20online%20games) more than the rating alone when it comes to online multiplayer games.

The "Everyone Else's Parents Let Them" Problem

About 60% of kids ages 12-14 have played M-rated games, according to various surveys. So yes, your kid is probably telling the truth when they say "everyone" is playing [Call of Duty](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/call-of-duty-game).

That doesn't mean you have to say yes. But it does mean you should:

1. **Actually understand what's in the game** (not just react to the M rating)
2. **Have a real conversation** about why you're saying yes or no
3. **Consider alternatives** that scratch the same itch but are more age-appropriate

If your 13-year-old wants [Call of Duty](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/call-of-duty-game), maybe [Fortnite](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/fortnite-game) or [Apex Legends](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/apex-legends-game) (both T-rated) could work instead. If they want [Grand Theft Auto](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/grand-theft-auto-game), maybe [Spider-Man](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/spider-man-game) or [Batman: Arkham](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/batman-arkham-game) games offer similar open-world action without the criminal glorification.

Age-Appropriate Guidance by Grade

**Elementary (K-5)**: Stick with E and E10+ games. Most kids this age aren't ready for realistic violence or complex themes, even if they think they are. [Mario](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/super-mario-game), [Minecraft](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/minecraft-game), [Splatoon](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/splatoon-game), [Animal Crossing](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/animal-crossing-game) are all solid choices.

**Middle School (6-8)**: T-rated games become appropriate for many kids, but not all T-rated games are created equal. [Fortnite](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/fortnite-game) at 11? Probably fine for most families. [Assassin's Creed](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/assassin-s-creed-game) at 11? Maybe wait a year or two. Check those content descriptors.

**High School (9-12)**: Most teens can handle T-rated content easily. M-rated games are a family-by-family decision. Some 14-year-olds are mature enough for certain M-rated games (especially those rated M primarily for violence rather than sexual content or drug use). Others aren't ready until 16 or 17.

How to Use Ratings Effectively

1. **Check the rating before you buy** (obviously)
2. **Read the content descriptors** on the back or on the ESRB website
3. **Watch gameplay videos** on YouTube to see what the game actually looks like
4. **Read parent reviews** on Common Sense Media or Screenwise
5. **Play with your kid** when possible, especially for new games
6. **Revisit your rules** as your kids mature

What Parents Should Know

The rating systems aren't perfect. They tend to be more lenient with violence than with sexual content (a very American thing). They don't account for the addictive nature of some games, predatory monetization, or online toxicity.

But they're still useful. A game rated E10+ is genuinely different from a game rated M. The system works if you actually use it.

Also: **ratings are assigned by playing through the game, but some content might be hidden or unlockable.** The ESRB relies on publishers to disclose all pertinent content, but occasionally something slips through. This is rare, but it's why staying involved matters.

The Bottom Line

ESRB and PEGI ratings are like nutrition labels for games. They won't tell you everything, but they give you enough information to make an informed decision. The age rating is your starting point. The content descriptors are your real guide.

When your kid asks for a new game:

1. Check the rating
2. Read what content earned that rating
3. Watch a gameplay video if you're unsure
4. Make a decision based on your family's values and your individual kid's maturity

And remember: saying no to one game doesn't mean saying no to gaming. There are thousands of games out there. [Help your kid find ones that match both their interests and your comfort level![](/favicons/favicon-32x32.png)](https://chat.screenwiseapp.com/?prompt=age%20appropriate%20game%20recommendations%20for%20my%20kid).

The ratings exist to help you, not to make you feel like a bad parent for letting your 12-year-old play [Fortnite](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/fortnite-game) or for saying no to [GTA](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/grand-theft-auto-game) for your 15-year-old. Use them as a tool, not a rulebook.

Next Steps

* Browse [age-appropriate games for your kids](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/age-appropriate-games-for-kids)
* Learn about [setting up parental controls on gaming consoles](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/parental-controls-for-gaming-consoles)

### SHOULD be 5 stars, BUT...

I love Apple Arcade. It’s got something for everyone and it’s really inexpensive.This game is \*beautiful\* and smart and fun but also kind of meditative while not being annoyingly easy OR too hard to be fun.It’s really really great. BUT it has one fatal flaw.Now, I see people complaining about the controls — I agree they could be a little better but it’s in no way something that I would take off points for. They’re not ~perfect~ but they’re certainly not an actual issue.I also see some people complaining about some of the puzzles/levels being too hard. That’s crazy. UNLESS you like your puzzle games to be entirely unchallenging so you can just go through the motions of doing the puzzles without really thinking. This is totally not a ~hard~ game. You just have to actually think for a minute and use some trial and error sometimes.THE PROBLEM IS:This game. Is SO SO SHORT!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!It almost feels likeeee a super-deluxe version of a demo or something. I’ve been finding it harder and harder to stumble upon Apple Arcade games that I haven’t played yet but really like, so this morning I was so stoked when I started playing this.I just checked my usage to make sure, I’m not exaggerating whatsoever. Honestly this is probably conservative because I know there were at least a couple of times that I got busy and set it down for a few minutes without closing it or shutting my phone off.LESS THAN 2 HOURS !L E G O !A P P L E !Honestly kinda shocked they didn’t make a longer game than this.But!!It’s still worth playing — it really is great.Just don’t start getting all cozy with it like you’re gonna be playing this thing for weeks or anything like that.

### Lego for Grownups

A few years ago I got a good deal on a large Wall-E Lego set and it transported me right back to my younger years. It was fun and challenging to put together, and the whole experience awoke the inner child in me. Seeing the finished product was so satisfying. In fact he’s still on my bookshelf on constant lookout to make sure my inner child doesn’t go back to sleep.Then in walks this new game to the Apple Arcade. It’s a stunning, much more mature and refined reinvention of the Lego game franchise and it’s breathtaking. No hokey Marvel tie-ins, no goofy characters. Think Monument Valley with 3D graphics and dynamic lighting that is so beautiful you’ll stop playing just to take it all in (fun tip: splash the “water” around for a surreal experience). It had the same effect my Wall-E Lego had on me, capturing my attention in a way very few things can manage.It’s a frustratingly short experience, but absolutely worth your while. I hope Lego realizes the potential here and expands this into a new franchise. Even the short playthrough was captivating and moving enough to melt me; I uttered an audible warm-hearted squeal when the little guy found his hat again. Please Lego, for the love of all things holy, expand this into a full length game.
